item.title: Decomposing the Cost of Complexity Under Risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.09381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study preferences under risk when the probability structure of a lottery can affect value separately from its final prizes. Our first result characterizes perturbed expected utility representation in which lottery value separates into expected utility over prizes and an additive perturbation term depending only on the probability tree. The key behavioral restrictions are branch cancellation, which separates prize evaluation from probability structure, and within-tree dominance, which captures that evaluations within the same probability tree are simple and follow dominance. Strengthening branch cancellation to lottery cancellation, which extends the invariance requirement from common prizes to common sublotteries, characterizes additive separability of the perturbation across branches. We also characterize when the tree dependent perturbation term depends only on the number of distinct possible prizes: under weaker continuity requirements, adding same-support independence yields a support size representation for nondegenerate lotteries, and a certainty equivalent condition extends it to degenerate lotteries. Finally, concavity gives the perturbation term its interpretation as a complexity cost.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoge Dong, Lasse Mononen

item.title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
item.description: arXiv:2611.09399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.
item.dc:creator: Xiaomeng Guo, Fasheng Xu, Xiaoli Zhang

item.title: Optimal robust comonotonic risk sharing under operational constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.09452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Risk-sharing arrangements such as reinsurance programs and catastrophe pools must satisfy operational constraints, including capacity limits, attachment bands, retention rules and cession limits. Under distortion risk measures, the unconstrained optimum assigns each loss layer to the participant for whom that layer is least costly, but operational constraints break this layerwise rule, and there is no general method to compute the constrained optimum. We show that, for comonotonic allocations, the participants' distortion risk measures and the operational constraints are linear in the amount of each loss layer held by each participant, so the constrained risk-sharing problem on a discretized loss is a linear program that standard software can solve. Its dual gives supporting prices for the loss layers and the marginal value of relaxing each operational constraint. Where the set of binding constraints changes, the constrained optimal value can have a kink, and the smallest and largest optimal multipliers then give the one-sided effects of relaxing and tightening a constraint. To protect the allocation against disagreement between loss models, we also consider the robust version of the risk-sharing problem, that is, minimizing the worst-case total risk assessment over finitely many probability scenarios. This robust problem is again a linear program, and we quantify the cost of protection against model uncertainty from its optimal value. We illustrate the approach with a catastrophe reinsurance tower.
item.dc:creator: Carole Bernard, Christopher Blier-Wong, Jean-Gabriel Lauzier

item.title: Moral Consumers and the Environment
item.description: arXiv:2611.09515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the taxation of environmentally harmful goods when consumers have a Kantian desire to ``do the right thing''. A consumer evaluates her buying strategy, a rule that specifies whether to buy, by the material payoff she would obtain if others followed the same rule with a probability given by her degree of morality. Equilibrium exists and is unique in finite populations with heterogeneous morality. The optimal tax depends crucially on whether consumers are aware that tax revenue is returned to them. If they are, the Pigovian tax is optimal under homogeneous morality, whatever consumers know about environmental costs, and we give conditions under which it remains the unique optimum under heterogeneous morality. If they are not, the optimal tax is lower, and more so the more moral consumers are. Under a quota system such as the EU Emissions Trading System, any cap at least as stringent as the Pigovian quota admits an equilibrium in which morality has no effect on consumers who are aware of the system.
item.dc:creator: Mogens Fosgerau, J\"orgen Weibull

item.title: Who Picks First? Compensatory Fairness When Equal Division Is Impossible
item.description: arXiv:2611.09685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When indivisible objects, such as heirlooms or tickets to sports events, do not divide evenly among agents with equal claims, some agents must receive more objects than others. Can picking first compensate those with fewer objects? We propose two principles of compensatory fairness. An agent with fewer objects must not envy a larger bundle with any one of its objects removed, and priority advantages among agents with equally many objects must alternate rather than accumulate. Non-wastefulness, neutrality and an object-wise form of Maskin monotonicity characterize the draft rules, in which agents pick in a fixed sequence. Adding the two principles and envy-freeness up to one object singles out the block--snake draft, in which agents with fewer objects pick first in every round and each group's order reverses between rounds. Among draft rules, compensation is compatible with strategy-proofness, but envy-freeness up to one object is not: once at least two agents receive more than one object, no draft that satisfies it is even weakly strategy-proof, and with two such agents the conflict extends to all non-wasteful and neutral rules. When agents may be indifferent between objects, resolving each tie in favor of the earliest later picker who strictly cares preserves the draft's fairness guarantees and ensures efficiency under pairwise dominance.
item.dc:creator: Aleksei Chernulich, M. Bumin Yenmez

item.title: A Sequential Foundation for Two-Level Nested Logit
item.description: arXiv:2610.38098v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I show that the two-level nested logit model arises exactly from a sequential choice process in which group, subgroup, and product shocks are revealed in stages. The result extends to any number of levels and holds for any nesting parameters below one, without the bounds and ordering that random utility maximization requires. Parameter estimates that applied work discards for violating the standard ordering or the lower bound are consistent with sequential choice. The linear inversion and welfare formula hold. When the standard ordering fails, improving one product can raise a rival's market share in its subgroup, even with single-unit demand.
item.dc:creator: Davide Luparello

item.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
item.description: arXiv:2611.02984v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.
item.dc:creator: Federico Fioravanti, Leo Kurata, Vasilis Stamatis

item.title: Effective Horizons for Prophet Inequalities with Discounted I.I.D. Rewards
item.description: arXiv:2606.30118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study prophet inequalities for $n$ i.i.d. base rewards subject to multiplicative discounts across $S$ phases. For equal-length phases and a common discount factor $\widetilde\gamma$, we characterize the optimal competitive ratio of single-quantile policies as $n\to\infty$ with $S$ and $\widetilde\gamma$ fixed. The resulting sharp guarantee describes the dependence on the phase parameters: it recovers $1-1/e$ without discounting and approaches $1/2$ in the worst-case regime. We also establish a distribution-free comparison that bounds the discounted prophet by a fractional i.i.d. maximum with effective horizon $B$, the sum of the discount weights across all observations. The comparison yields acceptance probability $1/B$, determined only by the phase profile. This calibration attains the canonical optimum even among single-quantile policies that may choose their acceptance probability using the known base distribution. The comparison also gives guarantees for heterogeneous discounts and unequal phase lengths. A complementary optimal-stopping upper bound establishes the same limiting optimum of $1/2$ for arbitrary stopping rules in the canonical model. Finally, the same effective-horizon calibration sets acceptance probability $1-\widetilde\gamma$ under infinite-horizon geometric discounting. This explicit quantile rule attains Boshuizen's (1994) known optimal worst-case ratio $1/(1+\widetilde\gamma)$ without solving a Bellman equation.
item.dc:creator: Jung-hun Kim, Vianney Perchet
